title: Geographically explicit event models and niche dynamics: unravelling the diversification of the Nearctic–Neotropical clade Tetyra+Kernegaster (Hemiptera: Scutelleridae)
content:
Abstract
The aim of this study was to integrate historical biogeographical and climatic macroecological perspectives within a phylogenetic framework to elucidate how past geographical events and environmental differentiation have jointly shaped distributional patterns and niche evolution in the Northern Hemisphere genus Tetyra and the Neotropical genus Kernegaster in the Americas (50°N–60°S). For the three species of Tetyra and nine species of Kernegaster (Scutelleridae: Pachycorinae), we used the geographically explicit event model (GEM) to reconstruct ancestral ranges and cladogenetic modes without predefined areas. Environmental principal component analyses (PCA-env) were implemented to quantify realized niche overlap and test for phylogenetic niche conservatism using background similarity tests and the environmental occupancy index. Complementarily, spatial evolutionary and ecological vicariance analysis (SEEVA) was used as a nodal diagnostic to pinpoint specific climatic dimensions driving ecological vicariance. GEM results showed a prevalence of basal vicariance events, with derived speciation events dominated by founder events and sympatry. In Tetyra, PCA-env revealed significant niche shifts between allopatric species, yet background similarity tests confirmed that lineages actively track a conserved climatic core. Conversely, SEEVA recovered universal shifts across almost all variables at Tetyra nodes, identifying regional specialization. In Kernegaster, the realized niche space was structured into two distinct ecological assemblages: a restricted, seasonal group associated with the Atlantic Forest, and a broader generalist group. Similarity tests supported a ‘jump speciation’ model for Kernegaster multimaculatus, which underwent radical niche shifts relative to its sister taxon. SEEVA identified punctual and mild vicariance in precipitation and temperature variables in three Kernegaster nodes, associated with major disjunctions and a shift in niche preference. In conclusion, speciation in Tetyra was driven primarily by geographical isolation rather than ecological innovation; the recovered phylogenetic niche conservatism suggested that lineages adapted to regional environments while remaining tethered to an ancestral niche core. Kernegaster displayed a more heterogeneous evolutionary trajectory, characterized by allopatries and steady conservatism in early branches, followed by niche divergence in the Atlantic Forest endemic species and a recolonization of a plesiomorphic environmental optimum in K. multimaculatus. Together, these results demonstrate that niche evolution of the group is driven mainly by major historical events and adaptive specialization to regional climate filters.
